column4: The section’s cited ط ع م root covers food, feeding, and hospitality, and it names the orphan and poor as those left without it; 76:8 depicts feeding the poor, orphan, and captive while the givers themselves love the food, turning withheld household provision into costly care.

The section cites 76:8 as food given to the poor and orphan despite the givers’ love of it; 76:9 continues that same meal scene and says they feed for God’s sake without seeking repayment or thanks, clarifying the motive behind the provision.

The section’s named طَعَام and root ط ع م link food to feeding; here Moses and his companion ask the town’s people for food, and they refuse to host them (فَأَبَوْا أَن يُضَيِّفُوهُمَا), a concrete scene of denied hospitality.

The source section defines the orphan as a child whose father has died and describes him being pushed away; 89:17 names failure to honor the orphan, directly setting that treatment against the duty the scene violates.

The section quotes the root ط ع م for food and feeding and says the man does not urge food for the poor; 89:18 likewise rebukes people for not urging one another to feed the poor, a close formulation of the image’s neglected encouragement.
The section’s cited wording ولا يحض على طعام المسكين is repeated in 69:34 as part of the account of the people of the left; this ayah makes the refusal to urge feeding the poor an explicit charge.

The section’s ط ع م root links household food with feeding a person who asks; 36:47 stages the refusal itself: the deniers answer that they should feed someone God could feed, exposing the excuse behind withholding.

The section connects household stores and the small kindness of al-maʿūn with recognized good; 4:8 says that when relatives, orphans, and the poor attend an inheritance division, they should receive a share and kind words, making provision in the household setting concrete.

The section imagines a neighbor coming to the door for food or a useful household object; 4:36 specifically commands good treatment of the near and distant neighbor, alongside the orphan, needy, and traveler, locating the small domestic kindness within neighborly duty.

The source section’s ط ع م root names food and feeding and its scene names the orphan and poor; 2:177 describes giving wealth, despite love for it, to relatives, orphans, the needy, travelers, and askers, showing what the withheld provision could become.

The section describes the orphan as a fatherless child treated as an outsider and pushed away; 2:220 says that improving the orphans’ affairs is best and that mixing with them makes them brothers, directly answering the image’s exclusion from the household.

The source section’s dictionary gloss for يَتِيم identifies the child whose father has died; 93:6 recalls God finding the Prophet an orphan and giving shelter (فَآوَى), a direct counterimage to pushing the fatherless child away.
The section’s named word ٱلْيَتِيم is the orphan whom the man pushes; 93:9 gives the explicit boundary فَلَا تَقْهَرْ, not to oppress the orphan, reversing the act in the image.

The section describes the orphan inside a household from which care and provision are withheld; 18:82 reveals that the wall and hidden treasure belong to two orphan boys and are preserved for them because their father was righteous, a specific case of safeguarding an orphan household’s future.

The section’s named orphan is a child whose household provision is vulnerable; 17:34 sets a boundary around approaching an orphan’s property except in the best manner until maturity, completing the neighboring measure command in 17:35 with a rule against taking from the child.

The section’s cited dictionary form دعدع مكيالا describes shaking a measure until it is full; 17:35 commands full measure and fair weighing, completing 17:34’s protection of the orphan’s property with fair dealing in provisions.

The section joins the orphan to the filling and measuring of household food; 6:152 puts both concerns in one command, protecting an orphan’s property until maturity and requiring full measure and just weight, so a child’s due and a measured allotment meet in the same ayah.

The source section’s cited dictionary form دعدع مكيالا is shaking a measure so it contains the full amount; 83:3 gives the opposite practice, shorting people when measuring or weighing, making the image’s filling and withholding a question of another person’s due.

The section names م ن ع as the root of withholding and cites the filled measure; in 12:63 the brothers say مُنِعَ مِنَّا الْكَيْلُ, that the ration is withheld from them. In its context they need another family provision from Egypt and ask to take Benjamin so they can measure grain again, tying refusal to household food.

The section cites the س ك ن root for a home, its people, and what lets people dwell there; 16:80 says God made homes سَكَنًا, a place of settlement, giving the domestic word behind the poor person’s name a concrete Quranic home scene.

The section’s food image is household nourishment withheld from the needy; 90:14 names the act of feeding on a day of hunger, making the provision concrete rather than an abstract gift. Verses 90:15–16 specify the orphan and person in misery.
This ayah names an orphan who is a near relative as a recipient of the difficult ascent; 90:14 supplies the feeding scene, while this verse makes kinship and orphanhood part of who receives care.

This ayah names a poor person in misery as a recipient of the difficult ascent; 90:14 supplies the feeding action, and this verse specifies the vulnerable person who corresponds to the section’s poor at the door.
The source section centers food for the poor and the refusal to offer it; in 74:44 the people of the Fire name not feeding the poor among their own failures, giving the omission a stated consequence.

The section’s household scene has a person guarding useful things and food from someone who asks; the garden owners in 68:24 explicitly resolve that no poor person should enter to collect its fruit, a close parallel of planned exclusion from provision.

The section shows goods kept back from a needy visitor; after the garden owners bar the poor in 68:24, 68:25 shows them setting out early with determined purpose to harvest, completing the deliberate withholding scene.

The section describes a household host and vessels used to serve food; 51:27 shows Abraham placing the calf before his guests and inviting them to eat, a direct scene of open hospitality against the refused guest and asker.

The source section’s cited dictionary gloss for طاعم and مطعام describes a host who receives guests generously; 51:26 shows Abraham going to his household and bringing a fat calf, the preparation that makes the meal in 51:27 possible.
The section’s host gloss centers the people received in a household; 51:24 names Abraham’s honored guests, identifying the visitors whose meal and welcome continue in 51:26–27.

The section defines the orphan as fatherless until maturity; 4:6 describes testing orphans until they reach marriageable age and then handing over their property if sound, giving a practical household-care boundary to that definition.

The section depicts the fatherless child kept from household provision; 4:2 commands guardians to give orphans their property and not consume it with their own, extending care from food and small goods to the child’s estate.
The section’s orphan is denied what a household should offer; 4:10 names consuming orphans’ property unjustly as swallowing fire, a sharp reversal of the care and provision the child lacks.

The section makes household food and small supplies the means of care for the vulnerable; 2:215 answers what to spend by naming parents, relatives, orphans, the needy, and travelers, specifying recipients for such provision.

The section imagines a small household benefit being asked for by someone nearby; 17:26 orders giving relatives, the needy, and the traveler their due, translating the stored household resource into a duty to provide.

The section’s needy person comes to ask at the door and receives no encouragement; 17:28 addresses turning away from needy relatives, poor, or travelers when one lacks means and commands a gracious word, preserving kindness even when one cannot give.

The section names withholding through root م ن ع and describes a hand that grips small useful things; 17:29 pictures the hand tied to the neck as stinginess and sets it against reckless spending, making the closed hand visible.

The section’s small household kindness is kept from a person in need; 24:22 tells people of means not to swear off giving to poor relatives and emigrants, but to pardon and continue giving, a specific case of reopening support after a grievance.

The section’s hand withholds ordinary household benefits from a neighbor; 59:9 describes the Helpers welcoming newcomers and preferring them with their resources even when they themselves are needy, the household ethic’s opposite.

The section’s cited root glosses س ك ن as house and household and describes food that sustains a place; 24:61 names eating in one another’s homes and the homes of relatives and friends, a concrete Quranic scene of shared food across households.

The section develops the home as the place where a host prepares food for guests; 33:53 describes guests entering the Prophet’s home, eating when invited, and leaving afterward, giving a domestic boundary around hospitality.

The source section glosses م ع ن as small, easy household benefit and as recognized good; 51:19 says that in the righteous people’s wealth is a known right for the asker and deprived person, making even a small share a claim rather than mere favor.

The section depicts practical goods and food kept from people in need; 70:24 says a known right is set within the believers’ wealth, and 70:25 identifies the asker and deprived person, completing who holds that right.

This ayah identifies the beneficiaries of the wealth right in 70:24 as the asker and deprived; it makes the section’s person coming to request a pot, water, or food recognizable as a claimant to provision.

The section contrasts keeping food and household goods with giving them; 3:92 says righteousness is not attained until one gives from what one loves, a specific bridge to the loved food in 76:8 and the small things held back here.

The section cites م ن ع and glosses its miserly form as a person who is stingy and holds back; 4:37 depicts those who are stingy, urge stinginess, and conceal God’s bounty, closely matching the named disposition and hidden stores.

The source section’s dictionary gloss for م ن ع describes the miserly person as holding back; 9:76 shows people who, after receiving bounty, become stingy with it and turn away, making the withholding an action rather than only a label.
The section explicitly names a miserly, withholding person through root م ن ع; 57:24 describes people who are stingy and urge others to stinginess, a direct parallel to the disposition in the image.
The section shows household goods held back from the needy; 3:180 rejects the idea that withholding what God has given is good and pictures that hoarded bounty as a collar on the Day of Resurrection.
The section’s named root م ن ع makes withholding the central act; 47:38 contrasts the call to spend with whoever then withholds, and says that withholding harms the person who does it.

The section’s image turns on a hand so closed it refuses even a small, useful object; 25:67 sets the believers’ spending between extravagance and stinginess, giving a boundary for household giving rather than endorsing the closed hand.

The section links grain, a filled measure, and food for the needy; 6:141 speaks of eating the crop when it bears fruit and giving its due on harvest day, connecting provision directly to distribution.

The section describes grain settling in a shaken measure until more fits and the bowl fills; 2:261 also uses grain growing into abundant provision, though its point is the multiplied reward of spending rather than filling a household vessel.

The section’s cited dictionary form دعدع مكيالا means shaking a measure to take its full contents; 55:9 commands establishing weight with justice and not making the balance deficient, directly bounding the measure image.

The section develops filling and measuring a vessel; 55:8 says not to transgress in the balance, while 55:9 specifies not making it deficient, so this verse supplies the broader boundary around the next ayah’s measure.

The section’s measure is shaken until the full amount settles; 83:1 announces woe for the mutaffifin, and 83:2–3 specify their practice of taking full measure but giving less, reversing the filled measure.

The section’s image is a measure filled to capacity; 83:2 describes people who take full measure for themselves, and 83:3 supplies the corresponding short measure they give others, exposing the asymmetry.

The section names pots and useful household objects, and also develops grain being shaken into a measure; 12:70 places Joseph’s cup in a brother’s bag after provisioning the family, joining a concrete vessel to a ration scene, though here it serves a plot rather than a loan.

This ayah identifies the missing object in the scene begun at 12:70 as the king’s measuring cup and offers a camel-load to its finder; it links a household vessel with measured food provision, while its royal setting differs from the neighbor’s small loan.

The section’s dish, pot, and other household utensils are shown empty or full according to how people share; 76:15 depicts silver vessels and glass cups being passed among the people of Paradise, a concrete Quranic scene of vessels in circulation.
The section develops shaking a measure until the container is full; 76:16 describes clear cups of silver measured in precise proportion, completing the vessels in 76:15 with an explicit measure.
The section’s household containers are for food or drink; 76:17 continues the serving scene with a cup mixed with ginger, showing the vessels in 76:15–16 carrying a drink.
This ayah names the spring from which the cup in 76:17 is mixed; it completes the provision scene attached to measured cups, though the spring itself is not a household object.

The section describes everyday bowls and useful household vessels and asks what it means to withhold them; 43:71 depicts trays of gold and cups circulated among the people of Paradise, a specific image of shared vessels and provision.

The section names a shelf of useful household things and a bowl filled with food; 56:18 pictures cups, ewers, and a drink vessel circulated among the people of Paradise, a concrete scene of serving vessels in use.

The section’s household utensils are useful because they pass between people with food and drink; 52:23 depicts a cup passed among the people of Paradise, making circulation of a shared vessel explicit.
The section describes filling and serving from a vessel; 37:45 shows a cup of pure drink circulated among the people of Paradise, a specific scene of provision passed from hand to hand.

In the oath-expiration rule, this ayah requires feeding ten poor people from the average food one gives one’s own household. That is a concrete household-to-poor transfer matching the section’s filled bowl and food for the miskin.

The section’s al-maʿūn list names useful everyday household things; 2:267 warns against selecting for charity what the giver would accept only with eyes closed, a specific standard for the quality of goods shared.

The brothers find their traded goods returned in their baggage and say they can now obtain provisions for their family. This is not a borrowed pot, but it is a specific, indirect parallel to the section’s claim that small goods given from a household often return while the household gets what it needs.

After the provisions and hidden cup of 12:70, the brothers turn back and ask what is missing; 12:72 names the king’s cup. The section’s inventory of loanable household objects has a concrete, though royal and accusatory, counterpart in this missing vessel.

The section depicts a householder withholding small material benefits; 16:71 asks why those favored in provision would not share their provision with those under their authority, making withheld household resources a concrete analogy in its argument against denying God’s favor.

This ayah repeats the provision-sharing comparison in 16:71 as a question about whether people would accept those under their authority as equal partners in their provision; it sharpens the section’s closed-hand image into a question of who is allowed a share.

The ayah allocates a share of war gains to orphans, the needy, and the traveler; it gives a concrete instance of household-like resources being directed to the very vulnerable recipients whom the section’s man leaves without support.

The ayah assigns communal wealth to relatives, orphans, the needy, and travelers so it will not circulate only among the rich; this directly counters the section’s image of useful provisions kept within one household.

The section defines the orphan as a child left fatherless and makes the home’s provisions part of that child’s vulnerability; 4:9 asks people handling inheritance to imagine leaving weak offspring behind and fear for them, between 4:8’s instruction to give and 4:10’s warning against consuming orphan property.

This ayah addresses orphan girls whose guardians withhold what is due to them and commands justice toward vulnerable children; it extends the section’s fatherless-child scene from food and shelter to the guardian’s duty not to deny her rights.

The disciples ask Jesus for a table spread with food from heaven; the section names the sofra cloth among ordinary household goods and develops food placed in a filled bowl, so this is a direct table-and-meal scene.
This ayah says the disciples want to eat from the table and have their hearts reassured; it completes the request in 5:112 by stating the meal’s role for those who will share it.
Jesus asks for a table to be sent down as a feast for the first and last of them; this ayah supplies the communal meal requested in 5:112 and connects a shared table with provision.

God answers that the table will be sent down and sets a severe boundary for anyone who disbelieves afterward; it completes 5:112–114’s scene of provision with the consequence attached to receiving it.

The section’s cited household-benefit list includes a knife among ordinary items that may be borrowed; 12:31 places knives in the women’s hands during a gathering at the house, a specific domestic-use scene for one of those small tools.

The section identifies a withholding man as stingy and tight-fisted; 92:8 describes one who is stingy and thinks himself self-sufficient, giving a specific account of the attitude behind keeping small household benefits back.

After the stingy person of 92:8, this ayah says he denies the best; it adds the refusal that leads into the consequence in 92:10, matching the section’s act of withholding rather than merely its household setting.

This ayah allows a feeding ransom for a poor person in the context of fasting; it is a concrete measured food provision for a miskin, matching the section’s link between food and the person left without it.

For a hunting violation during pilgrimage, this ayah allows an expiation by feeding needy people; the specific food-for-needy provision offers another concrete instance of the transfer the section’s withholding scene suppresses.
This ayah requires feeding sixty poor people when the prescribed fast cannot be performed; the measured number and meal make the section’s food for the miskin a specific act of provision.

The section defines the orphan as a child whose father has died and places household food under that child’s care; 2:233 assigns the nursing mother’s food and clothing to the father, showing the household support whose loss makes the orphan vulnerable.
